newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik guerrillas agree to free UN hostages - govt.
newsitem.headline: Tajik guerrillas agree to free UN hostages - govt.

text.p: Tajikistan said on Saturday it had reached agreement with a guerrilla group for the release of seven United Nations military observers and 15 other hostages seized and held under threat of death.

Amirkul Azimov, Secretary of Tajikistan's Security Council, told Reuters the guerrillas, who say they are loyal to field commander Rizvon Sadirov, had agreed to free all hostages after all-night talks with government representatives.

He gave no details and did not say precisely where or when the hostages would be released. U.N. sources said the captives included two Bulgarians, a Dane, a Jordanian, a Ukrainian, a Uruguayan and an Austrian.

Sadirov had until recently been allied with the Islamic rebel opposition to President Imomali Rakhmonov, but switched to back the government of the former Soviet Republic, apparently without surrendering control of his forces.

A U.N. source in Dushanbe, capital of the former Soviet republic, told Reuters the guerrillas held up a column carrying U.N. personnel, Tajik officials and members of the armed Islamic opposition on Friday.

The hostage-takers demanded the rebels free Sadirov's brother, who is held by opposition fighters in the mountainous Tavildara region. Sadirov himself is believed to be in Afghanistan with groups of armed followers.
They also said that Russian border guards, thousands of whom have a peacekeeping role in Tajikistan, must provide safe passage for Sadirov's fighters to join them from bases across the Afghan border.
They said they would shoot their hostages and detonate 30 bombs hidden around Dushanbe unless their demands were met by two p.m. (0900 GMT) on Sunday.

In Moscow, talks between Rakhmonov and the head of an opposition delegation, Sayid Abdullo Nuri, aimed at ending four years of bloody civil war, continued without any apparent result and were due to resume on Saturday.
The U.N. source said the hostages included foreign and Tajik U.N. workers as well as government and opposition members of a joint committee set up to negotiate between the two sides.
In Copenhagen, a military statement identified the Dane as Major Jens Alsing, 36, and said the United Nations reported on Friday afternoon that he was in good condition.
It quoted the United Nations as saying that it was in touch with "parties in the area" and was negotiating for the hostages' release but it expected the negotiations to take several days.
The U.N. mission has 96 foreign military observers in Tajikistan. Its mandate was renewed last week for four months.
U.N. observers have twice this month been subject to beatings or mock executions at the hands of Tajik government soldiers.
Tens of thousands of people have been killed in four years of civil war between Tajikistan's secular government and Islamist guerrillas.
The warring sides agreed to the Moscow talks after meeting in Afghanistan this month. But shortly afterwards local officials reported fighting in the Garm region, 150 km (100 miles) east of Dushanbe.
Rakhmonov and Nuri met on Thursday and Friday in Moscow with the special U.N. envoy to Tajikistan, Gerd Merrem, and Russia's special envoy, Yevgeny Mikhailov, acting as mediators.
Rakhmonov's press secretary told Itar-Tass news agency an accord could be signed on Saturday if the two sides came to an agreement. But he made clear there were many outstanding issues.
Ceasefires agreed in the past have been routinely flouted, sometimes immediately after they were signed.
Russia, concerned about security on its volatile central Asian flank, has supported Rakhmonov's government but is also actively promoting peace talks with the opposition.
